analysis.one_liner: Lets sexual assault victims go to court instead of forced arbitration, with fairness rules for harassment arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received no committee or floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop companies from using pre-employment contracts to force employees with sexual assault claims into private arbitration instead of court. For sexual harassment claims, it would let arbitration continue only if the agreement met a list of fairness conditions, such as letting the worker speak publicly, report to law enforcement, bring a lawyer, and get a written decision. It would also limit the share of any recovery that the worker's attorney could take, and it would apply only to contracts signed after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who sign arbitration agreements as a condition of employment and later experience sexual assault on the job would get their day in court. Workers with harassment claims would keep the option of arbitration but gain guaranteed rights within it: public disclosure, referral to law enforcement, counsel, discovery, impartial arbitrators, and written decisions. Courts, rather than arbitrators, would decide whether the rules apply, and a worker who wins that challenge would recover attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with sexual assault or harassment claims

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements for sexual assault claims, so an employee alleging sexual assault could sue the employer in court instead of being locked into private arbitration.

For sexual harassment claims, an arbitration agreement is enforceable only if it lets the worker publicly discuss the claim and the outcome, report to law enforcement, use a lawyer, obtain third-party discovery, get an impartial arbitrator, receive a written reasoned decision, recover individualized damages, and avoid paying arbitration fees above federal court filing fees.
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies to an agreement, and a worker who successfully challenges an invalid agreement is awarded reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would lose the ability to keep sexual assault claims out of court and would face fair-process requirements and fee awards when their harassment arbitration agreements fall short. Arbitration providers would handle fewer cases on the old terms. Plaintiffs' attorneys would see their fees from these cases capped at a reasonable percentage of, and never more than, the client's actual recovery.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves forced arbitration in place for sexual harassment claims, requiring only fair procedures; it does not go as far as giving harassment claimants a choice of court, which was the approach in the broader ban Congress later enacted.

It caps the attorneys' fees a worker's lawyer can take from a sexual assault or harassment recovery, which civil attorneys' groups generally warn can make it harder for victims to find representation in lower-value cases.
It applies only to agreements entered into or amended after enactment, so workers already bound by existing arbitration contracts would get no help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers with sexual assault claims, the benefit is substantial: escaping forced arbitration restores access to court, public record, and appeal. The trade-offs are real but narrower: harassment claims stay in arbitration (with better safeguards), attorney fee caps could shrink the pool of lawyers willing to take these cases, and prospective-only application leaves existing contracts untouched. On balance the bill was a meaningful worker-protection measure, though weaker than the version that became law in March 2022, which banned forced arbitration for both assault and harassment claims.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Joni Ernst introduced the bill on November 2, 2021.
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Judiciary Committee; no hearing, markup, or vote followed.
Three Republican senators cosponsored the bill, and no other action occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration agreements and arbitration providers kept the status quo under this bill. The loss to workers was limited in practice, because Congress passed and the President signed a broader forced-arbitration ban for sexual assault and harassment claims in March 2022.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and arbitration firms kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Joni Ernst
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void forced arbitration for sexual assault claims and set fairness standards for harassment arbitration.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; held no hearing or markup and never reported the bill, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: Employers using mandatory arbitration agreements
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on forced arbitration of workplace sexual assault and harassment claims as the broader debate played out in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the Republican sponsor and her three cosponsors were all Republicans, while the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee simply never acted.

industries.note: They would lose the power to route sexual assault claims out of court and would have to rebuild harassment arbitration agreements to meet fair-process standards or lose them too. Keeping forced arbitration preserves employer control over how these disputes are heard.

Sexual assault claims would leave private arbitration for the courts, shrinking a lucrative caseload; harassment cases would stay but with fairness rules, fee caps, and court review of agreement validity.

The bill opens courtroom access for assault claims and pays fees for winning arbitration challenges, but it also caps attorney fees at a reasonable percentage of, and no more than, the client's actual recovery, which could deter representation in small-dollar cases.
